cultivar: Si Ji Chun, Jin Xuan or Qingxin, depending on the maker
processing: Withered leaf is held in a nitrogen-flushed, oxygen-free chamber in several cycles alternated with air (roughly 8–10 hours in total), which converts glutamic acid into GABA; it is then oxidised, pan-fired, ball-rolled and almost always roasted. A Taiwanese lot must contain at least 150 mg of GABA per 100 g of dry tea to carry the name.
harvest_season: Any season; much of it is made from summer and autumn lowland leaf, with spring lots a little brighter.
appearance_dry: Tight dark reddish-brown balls with a dull surface and a sweet-sour, dried-fruit smell.
appearance_wet: Soft brown-red leaves with darker edges, fully oxidised-looking for an oolong.
taste_profile: Tamarind, raisin, baked apple and dried apricot over a soft roasted body with a distinct tang on the finish; a good lot is like a dried-fruit compote, a poor one is flat or vinegary.

brewing.notes: Water just off the boil and relaxed steeps, or Western-style at 3 g per 250 ml for three minutes. Cold-brews well and takes a little honey happily. Do not expect a normal oolong.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's tea by maker rather than by garden, often with a laboratory analysis of the GABA content attached, which is worth asking for; roasted lots keep for several years and some makers sell two- or three-year-old tea as mellower. Cheap 'GABA' tea without the sour-fruit signature is sometimes ordinary roasted lowland oolong.
description:
GABA oolong is a Taiwanese tea defined by its processing rather than its origin: fresh leaf is held in an oxygen-free, nitrogen-flushed chamber before it is made into tea, which converts some of its glutamic acid into gamma-aminobutyric acid, the compound the tea is named and marketed for. The method was developed at Japan's national tea research institute from 1984 and sold there from the late 1980s as Gabaron; Taiwanese makers adapted it to rolled oolong, and Taiwan has since become the main home of GABA oolong, made mostly in the Nantou lowlands and in Taitung.

The leaf, usually Si Ji Chun, Jin Xuan or Qing Xin, is withered and then goes through several cycles of hours in the anaerobic tank alternated with air, roughly eight to ten hours in total, before being oxidised, pan-fired, ball-rolled and, almost always, roasted. The anaerobic step does something unusual to the flavour: it strips out the green florals and produces a sweet-sour, fruity character that no other process gives. Taiwan sets a minimum of 150 milligrams of GABA per 100 grams of dry tea for a lot to carry the name.

Expect tamarind, raisin, baked apple and dried apricot, a soft roasted body and a distinct tang on the finish; a good lot is like a dried-fruit compote, a poor one is flat or vinegary. Brew it with water just off the boil and relaxed steeps, or Western-style for three minutes; it also cold-brews well and takes a little honey happily. Do not expect a normal oolong. People who try it expecting Alishan are disappointed; people who like aged or heavily oxidised tea usually enjoy it.

It is sold as the current year's tea, by maker rather than by garden, and serious producers attach a laboratory analysis of the GABA content, which is worth asking for; cheap 'GABA' tea is sometimes ordinary roasted lowland oolong with none of the sour-fruit signature. Roasted lots keep for several years. The health claims around it run ahead of the evidence; drink it because you like the taste.

GABA black and GABA green are made the same way with different finishing, and the black is the gentler introduction.
history:
GABA tea began as research, not as a regional craft. In 1984 Dr. Tsushida and colleagues at Japan's national tea research institute started work on leaf held in an oxygen-free nitrogen chamber, where six to ten hours converted nearly all its glutamic acid to GABA while leaving catechins and caffeine as they were. By the late 1980s it was on sale in Japan, aimed at people with high blood pressure.

Taiwanese makers adopted the method and applied it to oolong, and today most GABA tea is associated with Taiwan.

Research on the health effects continues; a 2020 review found possible benefits for stress and sleep from oral GABA but called for more study.
